newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court says judge may consider acquittal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court says judge may consider acquittal.

text.p: The Supreme Court ruled Monday that a judge in handing down a sentence for a convicted criminal may take into account other conduct for which the defendant has been acquitted.

The justices, by a 7-2 vote, said the judge may consider it if government prosecutors have established the conduct by a "preponderance of the evidence" -- a less demanding standard than the clear and convincing proof needed for conviction.

"We hold that a jury's verdict of acquittal does not prevent the sentencing court from considering conduct underlying the acquitted charge, so long as that conduct has been proved by a preponderance of the evidence," it said.

The 10-page, unsigned ruling overturned two decisions by a U.S. appeals court in California. The other 11 appeals courts around the country have held that judges under federal sentencing guidelines could take the information into account.
Justice John Paul Stevens dissented, saying the law should be construed in view of the traditional requirement that criminal charges must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

"We should presume that Congress intended the new sentencing guidelines that it authorised in 1984 to adhere to longstanding procedural requirements enshrined in our constitutional jurisprudence," he said.
The ruling was a victory for the Justice Department.

In one case, a federal jury convicted a defendant of drug charges, but acquitted him of using a firearm in the offence. Despite the acquittal, the judge found a preponderance of evidence that he had possessed the gun during the offence.
The defendant was sentenced to 262 months in prison.
In the other case, a jury convicted a woman of one count of drug dealing, but acquitted her on the second count. The judge sentenced her to 27 months in prison.
The judge said he was not punishing her for the conduct for which she was acquitted, but that it was relevant in handing down the sentence.
